DISSOLUTION OF PARLIAMENT. Parliament was formally dissolved on Saturday (the 28th of March) by Royal Commission. The Lord Chancellor read the following speech : þÿ Mv Lords and Gentlemen, Wc are commanded by her Majesty to inform you that, in leleasmg you at tms early period from your attendance in Parliament, it is her þÿMajesty intention s immediately to dissolve the present Parliament, in order to ascertain in the most constitutional manner the sense of her people upon the present state of public affairs. Gentlemen of the House of Commons, We are commanded by her Majesty to thank you for the liberal provision which you have made for the exigencies of the public service during the period that will elapse before the

new Parliament, which her Majesty will direct immediately to be called, shall have been able to give its deliberate attenton to these matters. JAPAN. We last week published a telegraphic dispatch to tho effect that two British steamers had forced the entrance of the port of N.ingaski, in Japan. The following circumstances appear to have led to this step, which has been attended with excellent results. On the 11th of December, the two vessels, after having visited the ports of Simoda and Ilakodadi, presented themselve- before Nangasaki, but were refused admission by the Governor, a mandarin of high class. As this refusal amounted to a breach of the treaty concluded iu 1855, between Japan and England, as likewise between Japan and Russia, France and the United States, the two vessels steamed into the port and placed themselves abreast of the fortifications of the place, which are strong No resistance

was, however, offered by the Governor. On the following day the two Commanders left their vessels, and inarched to the residence of the Governor at the head of a numerous escort. The Governor refused \ to see them, but he acquainted the English I that any letter would be forwarded to the j Emperor at Jeddo. A letter was, consequently, dispatched to the Emperor, who ! received the remonstrance it contained in a , favourable manner, and replied in publish- ; ing an edict on the 26th of January, wherein j he gave orders that in future the three j ports mentioned above shall be opened to j the navies of England, France, Russia and j the United States. The crews of any foreign vessels are, however, forbidden to j penetrate into the interior of the country, j and any breach of this law will be punished i by imprisonment, the period of which is to be fixed by the Emperor himself.

KAFFIR CIVIL WAIL- TREMENDOUS SLAUGHTER By the mail-steamer England, which arrived at Dartmouth on Tuesday last, we have news from Natal relating to the disturbances among the Zulus. These disturbances were caused by a contest between Ketchwya and Unibulazi, two sons of the paramount Chief Panda. On the 2nd of December the latter was defeated with immense slaughter. The victorious Ketchwya, a lad of nineteen, after the battle divided his army into three sections, and with these scoured the country in all directions, putting to death not only his enemies, but also all neutral or doubtful subjects who came in his way. He, however, kept clear of the immediate vicinity of Panda, who, by the latest intel- j ligence was raising an army in defence of his j throne. It is said that the number of persons slaughtered by the victors must have been upwards of 30,000. '1 he latest accounts, which appear to be re- j liable as to the great fact, though somewhat confused in detail, state that Panda had re- I covered his power by ceding a large portion of territory to the Boers, who were assisting him against his rebellious son. Yesterday afternoon (says the IVat.nl Mercury of Dec. 27) a Dutch farmer named Van Staden came in direct from the Upper Zulu border, and brought the somewhat startling intelligence that þÿl anda has made over to the Boers the Zulu country from the Tugelato the White Umvulosi River nnd the sea, under a treaty of protection to Panda, who is to be guaranteed ! in the possession of his nominal sovereignty

The large slice of the Zulu country thus ceded comprises the most healthy and fertile portion of the whole, flanking the Natal border along its entire length, and having a commercial outlet on the coast at St. Lucia Bav. We have not heard what is to be done with Ketchwya, but presume he will share the fate of the weaker, now that a stronger than he has taken the field. The Boers it is stated, are hunting him from his hiding-place. Boers came in to the number of from 400 to 500 þÿ strong enough to dictate their own terms ; and we understand the ceded country will be speedily occupied by a large number of settlers from the Buffalo district and the more remote and inconvenient districts of the Transvaal. This new turn in Zulu affairs considerably complicates the difficulties of our colonial statesmanship, though we do not in the least apprehend that it increases, but rather diminishes, the danger of inroad or collision.

From the London Times AUSTRIA. Subjoined is a translation of the despatch which, on the 16th of March, was forwarded to Count Paar at Turin : þÿ <Sir, þÿ Directly after the return of the Emperor to his capital I took orders of His Majesty on the subject of Count þÿCavouv di s spatch ot the 20th of February, which was to serve as a reply to the reclamations you were charged to make to that Minister. 1 am at present aide to cuniinuui-: cate to you the impression which that document, produced on the mind of the Emperor, and to give you directions for the regulation of your conduct. þÿ The explanations offered by Count Cavour are far from having entirely satisfied us. That Minister publicly and plainly confesses that the Piedmoutese press has been guilty of excesses which are greatly to be regretted He openly condemns them. We willingly take note (prenons acte) of an avowal so candidly made, and duly appreciate the feeling which led to the declaration. Although we acknowledge the uniformity of our views on this point, wo are unable to subscribe to the inferences which M. de Cavour draws from his declaration. In fact, the President of the Council seems to think he is dispensed from all effort to repress those abuses of the press, the existence of which he acknowledg es, as soon as he has pointed out to are foreign Governments that judicial measures a sovereign remedy against them. He seems to be inclined to release himself from all responsibility, and to leave it entirely to the foreign Governments to take the initiative in the repression of

those excesses. ' This is not our view of things. The system proposed might suffice for the ordinary, 1 may say for the accidental, abuses from which the most respectable press is never quite free ; but we do not think this passiveness of the loeal Government is justifiable when the excesses ( ecarls ) of the press assume (as in the present ease) the form of a regular system of calling in question the validity of treaties, and when the viol nee and turpitude of the excesses are carried to such a pitch that revolt in a neighbouring country is openly preached, aud an apology is even made for regicide. We persist in thinking that in the presence of such enormities each Government is bound in honour anil duty to make its authority felt, and to prove by its acts that it is not only inclined to respect treaties itself, but to make them respected by its subjects. þÿ If we have properly understood the sense of Count þÿCavour reply, s that Minister seems to think we only complained of the polemics of the public papers, but our complaints bore reference also to the encouragement, as well open as tacit, which the press received from the attitude of the Government. þÿ Count Cavour gives us the assurance that he will not permit anything on the inonumn t which is to be erected at Turin to the Sardinian army that could give umbrage to our susceptibility or to that of our army. We regret that we were obliged to incite him to an assurance which, under all circumstances, would have been of

much treater importance if it had been given spontaneously. At the same time that we express our appreciation of the intention which led to such a declaration, we take the liberty of remarking, that M. de Cavour, when speaking of the simple proofs of sympathy which he has received from our Italian provinces and from other parts of the Peninsula, takes no notice whatever of the series of pretended deputations ( pretnidue deputations) which he has received in person. This appears to us to bo a most important fact, for, if it is noi of a nature to constitute a regular sucourageinent to revolt, it at least tends to relax those ties which unite legitimate Sovereigns and their subjects. It is true that M. de Cavour affirms, in the name of the Sardinian Government, that it is his firm intention completely to fulfill towards his neighbours the obligations and duties which the law of nations and treaties impose on him, but he will permit us to as ; if the tolerance which he displays towards a pre«s which incessantly attacks those territorial limitations that nrc consecrated by treaty is in keeping with his assurþÿances if the personal reception which he has given to numerous nddress s, all inspired by the hollow vision of Italian unity, and all tendiug to detach

s J\ C R 0 I X A V l, subjects from their duties towards their Governments þÿ is in accord with the letter and spirit of that treaty of peace, iu which the King of Sardinia renounced all claim aud pretension to the country situate beyond the limits ot Sardinia, as those limits were fixed by the final act of the Congress of Vienna ? Does Couut Cavour think that he well interpreted the internationa1 duties of Piedmout towards Austria, aud towards his other neighbours, when he received deputations and accepted addresses presented by foreign subjects, persons who are not bound by any particular tie to Sardinia? Does not his conscience reproach him with having, by these acts, encouraged evil passions, and furnished aliment for the ceaseless attacks of a malevolent press? þÿ On this point we have a right to expect explanations from M. de Cavour, as they alone can give us a just idea of the value which is to be attached to his protestations of respect for existing treaties. þÿ If we were disinclined to indulge in recriminations in respect to the past, and were willing to consider the assurance given by M de Cavour an indication of a more propitious future, that Minister has deprived us of the po-'ibility of doing so, for sitnu.tat.cously with 'he dciivtoy of his despatch the Correspundance Italien nr , lithographed at rutin, on the same day sj.it d a that the President of the Council find received deputation ofeitiz us from Modena and Reggio, who spoke of the ties which bound them to Pielmont, ties which were forcibly severed for

Or docs he think it would he proper ( loisible ) for us to seek redress for this attack on treaties by bringing an action against tl.c editor of a paper whose offence was that he had made mention of an action performed by the Minister of the King, or at least of one which he has never disavowed? þÿ Count Cavour indulges at length in recriminations relative to wrongs committed by the Austrian p css, which, il they w re well founded, would make no change in the nature of the control rsy. lint the reclamation which we have addressed to him furnishes him with no motive for remedying the evil we have pointed out. ANOTHER NEW DANCE. It seems that, in consequence of the unlooked-for success which lias attended the revival of the Lancers, a sense of mortified vanity aroused the great, professors of tho art to combine their efforts for the production of an entirely new quadrille, which should completely outshine its decrepit and insolent rival. Hence the new quadrille Cellarius, which combines every dance which has been the vogue of late years ; thus the Polka, the Deuxtemps, the Tarantelle, the Napolituirie, the Mazurka, and the Schottislie, are all danced by turns, and the effect is so pretty that

we can not help wondering that it has never been thought of before. At the private parties at the Tuileries this dance has met with the greatest favor ; the Empress being one of the best dancers of the Tarantelle, has allowed that figure to be dedicated to her, and called by her name.

A Proper Punishment for an Unnatural Mother. þÿ A person in rather a high position has just obtained from the Civil Tribunal of the Seine n separation front h's ... wife, consequence with the right of keeping his child, of the following circumstances:- a ho child had the measles, and its medical attendant declared its life to be in danger, but the mother nevertheless continued to prepare her toilette for un evening " party to which she had been in- vited. Yon cannot leave the child, who is dying," exclaimed the husband. The wife replied that it was impossible for Iter to remain away from the party without breaking her promise and being guilty of a want of politeness. The husband again remonstrated with her, but in vain ; she insisted on going to the party, if only for an hour. The hu-band then informed her that if sh" carried her intention into execution, the door would be closed against her on her return. The wife left for the party, but on her return home was refused admittance. The Tribunal has decided that the husband was perfectly justified, and has furthermore ruled that a wife who forsakes her child in illness forfeits her conjugal rights.

CHRISTIAN STED, ST. CROIX. FRIDAY, 1st MAY, 1857. The packet-schooner Rosaline left here on Tuesday afternoon last with our Mails to meet the homeward-bound steamer, Orinoco, at St. Thomas. Either the Parana or La Plata is 6aid to be the expected outward ship, and should it prove to be the latter vessel we may look for our European correspondence to-night or to-morrow morning, and if the former, on Sunday. We cannot, however, expect much in the shape of news by the coming mail, for we find that a dearth of politics reigns throughout Europe. The new British Parliament would only assemble this month ; therefore nothing definite can as yet be known as to the intended policy of Ministers in regard to China. Judging, however, from the latest telegraphic despatches received in England, it would appear that the existing difficulties between Great Britain and the Celestial Empire were likely to arrive at a pacific solution, as the Emperor is said to have discountenanced the acts of the Governor (Yeh) of Canton, and it is expected will cause reparation to be made for the conduct of his subjects.

Unreckoned Taxes. þÿ It is a fact worthy of consideration that all our good things in which mankind have either hand or voice musi! be paid for in some shape or other, every article over and above the original cost of time, talent or labour by which it was obtained. Fame, however well earned, pays a heavy impost to envy and general critisism. Rank and position pay a world of indirect taxes to public opinion and established custom, to what society expects, and what people will say. Our home pleasures must be paid for in family cares and anxieties, our social enjoyments in a thousand forms of conventionality, and our loves and friendships in many risks and forfeits. So life goes on teaching us that there is but one blessing " which maketb licit and addeth no sorrow."

FRANCE AND ENGLAND. Men like Napoleon, who believe mankind so void of common sense that they cannot be supposed to transact their own affairs without interference from the government, must often have occasion to groan over the official zeal of friends who, in their eagerness, are always proving too much. In order to extol the present Napoleonic system, every petty excrescence in the constitutional system of England is eagerly seized hold of by the semi-official journals. Thus, because some thousand men assemble in England and state their grievances, while in France, because they know there are 609,000 bayonets to put them down, no one dares so much as to lift his finger, it is inferred that France lives under a beneficial influence, which effectually prevents its exposure to such unseemly exhibitions

Elopement ok a Priest with his Penitent. þÿ One morning last week every newspaper office of Paris was visited by a government messenger, who, in breathless haste, forbade them to print a word of the news which had just arrived from Meaux. Call him by what name you will, Altdrew Jackson, Zaeliary Taylor, or James Buchanan, the President of the United States, with the power of appointment and the Veto power in his hands, can, if he chooses, hold in cheek the ultras of all the quarters and all sections. As for Mr. Buchanan, no man ever stood in a better position than he occupies to accomplish this very thing. The Democracy owes him a great deal more than they can possibly flatter themselves that he owes them. They could have elected no one else, and that they have elected hitn is owing to the Union feeling of the Central States. To this feeling, at that time strongly pervading the whole North, General Pierce owed his election too, but he never seems to have discovered it. We believe that Mr. Buchanan's optics are of a clearer sort. We believe that he is fully resolved that during his administration the Federal Government shall not be used for the purpose of promoting any sectional interest, but that, steadfastly adhering to the grand and truly American idea of local sovereignty, the great powers of the Union shall be firmly and impartially administered be.twcen the two sections of the country ; that the Federal Government shall occupy itself with its legitimate cares ; arid that its powers shall not be warped into a selfish, sectional, and . unconstitutional direction for the purpose of strengthening either part of the Union against th» other.

ITALY. A letter dated from the Abruzzi, m the kingdom of the Two Sicilies, the 22d of March, says that it would be impossible to give a true idea of the regime which prevails in those provinces, or of the sufferings endured by the inhabitants. Their liberties and lives are at the mercy of the commonest informer. A corporal of gendarmerie is as powerful as the King, and a judge of the third class is above the law. The writer of the letter mentions the following fact in corroboration of his statement: þÿ Monsignor Belgrado, Bishop of the diocess of Ascoli, in the Roman States, has within his jurisdiction a portion of the province of Aquila, in the kingdom of Naples. From time to time he makes a pastoral visit into that portion of his diocess. Some time since the Bishop, who was formerly Papal nuncio at the Hague, and who naturally receives the foreign journals, was visited by a young man at Civitaducale, who found in one of those foreign journals a strong article in disapprobation of the King of þÿNaples system of government. The young man was so imprudent as to mention this fact He was immediately arrested and cast into prison. After m uch suffering he was released, but on condition that he should not quit the town of Civitaducale. This restraint is still imposed on him, notwithstanding the intercession of Monsignor Belgrado, but a bishop is powerless against a police officer. Thus the most innocent action is converted into a crime, and the most trifling expression may entail on the
utterer the most violent persecution. ( From the Jamaica Despatch. April 24.) JAMAICA.

An unexpected and most Providential event has confirmed in a remarkable degree the grounds on which the remonstrances that are now proceeding from this Colony against the continuance of the African Slave Trade with Cuba have been based. The answer invariably returned by Government to Petitions and Memorials from the British Colonies on the subject of the public infraction of her Treaties for the suppression of the Slave Trade by Spain has been that thesa petitions have been based on a delusion, there being in fact no Slave Trade with Cuba which called for strong coercive measures. Hitherto we have been compelled to fall back on evidence supplied almost wholly by the American press ; and, although there probably could be no better secondary evidence in such a case than that of the press of a country whose ports were confessedly and notoriously the great nurseries of the trade ; still it was impossible not to feel that testimony of such a nature was liable to question in official bureaus, and required at least some confirmation in fact beforo it could be pressed with confidence, as conclusive of the bad faith of Spain. This confirmation has at length been afforded us at a most opportune moment. On Sunday the 12th inst., the Pinnace of II. M. Brig Arab, under the command of Lieutenant Stubbs, R. N., after a search of ten days in and about the keys on the South-side of Cuba, succeeded in capturing a schooner of 150 tons, name aud nation unknown, together with 370 slaves, survi-

vors of 500, shipped at. Kabinda on the Coast of Africa, and destined for disposal in Cuba. The circumstances of the capture are precisely these : On the 2nd of April, the pinnnoe left the 1 þÿArab off Trinidad do Cuba, in command of Lieut. Stubbs, a marine and 15 men, on a cruise On the 4th about half past one þÿo clock, the pinnace anchored in Boca Grande, where she found a Caytuanas Schooner, the þÿ Star , Captain McLauchlan, who informed Lieut Stubbs that there were three wrecks of slavers on þÿ Man-of- War þÿKey, off Boca Grande, front one of whioh Captain McLauchlan had obtained a small quan

tity of copper, about cue and a half miles east of Cape Breton ; the Slavers, the Captain stated, had been on shore for about two months. He also stated that on Cotton Keys he saw a wreck, and the lifeless bodies of about 2p Africans, in quite a perfect state. He also said that eight men, calling themselves fishermen, but evidently pilots, were on the west, point of Cay Grande, some of whom he knew, who informed him that they expected a vessel with Africaus to arrive daily. After this information, the pinnace cruised in the vicinity of Boco Grande, and returned. Captain McLauchlan then further informed Lieutenant Stubbs that these pilots were on the look-out there incessantly ; he also stated to him that a brigantiuc stood close iu to the land, and he (the captain) had ordered his men to go in search of the pinnace, should the brigt., prove to be a slaver ; the brigantine being certain that she was off' the Coast of Cuba, stood out to sea again. On the 9th, the pinnace weighed anchor, and ran round a poiut in order to elude the vigilance of þÿ the pilots of Cape Grande, On the 12th, at 9. 30 a.m., a schooner was observed from the pinnace running down with square sails set ; the pinnace immediately weighed and ran out and stood across the passage; at 10 a.m. the pinDace got her oars out ; and observed the schooner east off a boat that was being towed astern, and the schooner stood out to sea. The pinnace hoisted her colors and fired several shots across the þÿschooner bow s with Miuie rifles.

At 3 þÿo clock, the wind being light, oars were again put from the pinnace ; a marine, by the name of Baird, kept up a continual firing at the schooner. The schooner was now observed lowering a boat, and the firing was immediately directed against the boat, which completely shattered her rudder ; the boat then tossed up her oars, and this having been observed by the pinnace, as a token of surrender, Lieut. Stubbs oeased firing, and boarded the boat, and took the captain and his cook, and also his private adult slave, who had been concealed at the bottom of the boat ; a spy glass, and a lot of þÿColt revolv- s ers, loaded. By this time the schooner, with all sails set, was driving on to the reefs, the captain having lashed the helm up before quitting. The pinnace, on perceiving this, immediately left the boat and proceeded towards the schooner, which the Lieut, and his men boarded ; at that time she was about a hundred and fifty yards fiom the reef. He found 370 slaves on board, among whom were 42 females. Previous to the arrival on board the schooner, the slaves were all loosed on deck and one of them put her helm down, thus preventing L r going directly on the reef. The Schooner then ran down to Boco Grande, and anchored there. So many complaints having been heard in reference to the supposed illegality of the Postþÿmaster s charging full postage on letters to which stamps are affixed, but which nevertheless are marked þÿ þÿpaid, we think it may be of interest to our readers to translate that passage in the Circular to the Post Offices, issued by Government, which relates to such cases, Under the head þÿ postage þÿstamps we find the following : ' þÿ .As Paid' or þÿfranco in accordance with 9 of letters and packages, marked þÿ þÿfree the Postal Law, cannot be franked by stamps, every letter or package thus marked, shall in accordance with the law, be charged full postþÿage 4 cents pr. single þÿletter which postage must be paid by the sender, with a deduction of 3 cents for every stamp affixed, should it not be possible to obtain this postage from the sender, as in cases where such letters are deposited in the letter-boxes, the letter or package shall nevertheless be forwarded wiihout delay, charged however with the full postage

Alter cancelling the stamps on such letters &e., the Post Master shall mark on tbe left of tbe letter, under tbe address, with red ink, the word þÿ unpaid þÿ; and then affix his signature. The same manner of proceeding shall be observed, where either these words have evidently been smeared over with ink or erased, or wlien the stamp is fixed on the place, where such words are to be þÿwritten. No one can study the statistics relating to Frencu population, and compare its failing power oi increase with the progress of other nations, without being convinced that some great natural or social cause checks the vitality of tue whole people. It is not us if the diminution of increase were local, temporary, or dependent on certain political disorders ; it has been gradual and progressing, until now it seems that the total population is actually lessening. What makes the fact more singular is that such a condition of tilings is confined to I'miice. The great and never-ceasing increase of the English race is notorious, and need not further be dwelt Upon » but Germany and Russia have also shown no deficiency of prolific power. Although Muscovite statistics are hardly to be depended upon, it seems certain, from the testimony of travellers, that in the great territory of the Czar the human race is multiplying and extending. The progress of the Germans has been by no means unsatisfactory. It is true that narrow-minded Governments and obsolete laws have done their worst to check development, and that the Fatherland does not, in fact, gain as much as it should from the increase of its sturdy and laborious race. But the Germans have during the present generation become a great emigrating people. There has been no want of activity at home. America. The American Minister Extraordinary to China, Mr. W. B. Reed, will not, it is understood, proceed directly hence to Canton. He will embark in an early steamer for England, where he will communicate the purpose of his mission to the English Government, obtain the latest information of the state of atlairs, and learn what the policy of our Administration is to be ; he will then go to Paris, confer in the same manner with the French Government, and then pr oceed overland to Aden, where he will be met by the United þÿStates steamer which will take him to Canton. The main object of the American Government is to þÿ keep itself clear of an þÿ entangling a phrase which has produced a policy þÿalliance now become traditional, but it still has a power over the national sentiment, and that it might safely be departed from in some eases is not yet fully perceived. Adhering, therefore, to this policy, the Administration will not enter into any formal treaty with either England or Franco, or both combined. At the same time it feels and admits that the success of the English arms in China would promote the interests of America in that quarter of the world, in common with those of all the western nations. As much co-operation, therefore, moral or physical (in case of necessity), as may be consistent with the national policy will be furnished. The necessity, of course, will only arise if any Chinese outrage should endanger American life or property. The American squadron, though judiciously

reiiiforc d, will not, as a matter of course, immediately þÿ countþÿin if there should be fighting going on when the Mini. -tor arrives in which the ships already at Cuuton have not joined. These are contingencies, and the chapter of accidents may renþÿ der the policy of what may be called a co-operative þÿneutrality impracticable. At any rate, an armed force, and .lie authority that can direct its use, will be on the spot ; the rest is in the domains of time and events. Report speaks highly of the abilities and character of the new envoy, and the arrangement by which he will take London and Paris on the way to his destination is a very judicious one ; from his own Government he will receive powers, those of the belligerents will furnish him with information.

Our object in the present remarks is to warn the public against been led too easily into a ready acquiesence in any such measure. There are innumerable items in the yearly expenses of the Landtreasury where the pruning knife could do effectual service ; and, although we are personally aware, that a policy of retrenching small and necessary expenses, where the good of the public at large is concerned, while great and individual ones are allowed to pass unnoticed, is pursued, we must nevertheless advise the community individually and collectively, to institute a proper search into the affairs of the Commumal Treasury before any other steps are taken. Although commanded by the law of the 9th May 1865 23, the Burgher Council has published no statement of their Revenues and Expenses for the last year ; nor have they exhibited their yearly accounts for public inspection, as likewise prescribed by the law. Is it really a fact, as said of us, that we readily submit to any violation of our rights, even when we have the power to prevent it ? The public have a right to demand that these yearly statements be published ; and, if the new Communal Law be not already a dead letter, we expect to hear the reason why its injunctions are thus openly violated.

From the New York Herald , May 5. The New Granada þÿQuestion. Evils of Closing the Isthmus Routes þÿ The Duty of our Government. Our relations with New Granada have assumed a very serious aspect, and the question þÿ what course shall we now pursue in the matter ? þÿ is the mo-t prominent one that is presented for the decision of Mr. Buchanan and his Cabinet ; and it is more pregnant with good or evil results to our trade, our policy and our expansion, as lie may select, In other questions of the day. than any of the order to arrive at a just view of our position, and of the course we should pursue, a brief recapitulation o! the facts is neces-ary. On the 15th of April, 1856, a serious affray occurred in the suburbs of Panama þÿ no matter how originated þÿ which, from the want of a sufficient military or police force on the part of the government, assumed a serious character and resulted in the loss of several valuable lives and much property. The subsequent investigations by the authorized agents of the governments of the United States and New Granada assumed a partisan character and arrived at exaggerated results. Ou our side an intemperate course was officiously recommended by the Commissioner sent the to unwise ject ; and on the other, examine the sub- denial of a just responsibility was sustained by the government of New Granada. President Pierce, in his last annual message, added oil to the flame that had been created, by endorsing the ex parte statements that had be n laid before him, and by concurring in several gross errors

in relation to other existing questions with the government of New Granada This brought out a like exaggerated message from the President of that republic to the Granadian Congress. Coincident with these events Mr. Marcy drew up the project of a treaty to be made between the two governments, in which the just claims of our citizens were placed in a secondary position, and a virtual transfer of the sovereignty of a part of her territory was demand d of New Granada. Commissioners we,re appointed on both sides to discuss the questions at issue, and a correspondence ensued, in which, we must confess, that so far as regards a calm treatment of the subject, and the courtesies of diplomatic intercourse, our own Commissioners appear to a decided advantage. Those of New Granada declared that the step we desired that government to take

was unconstitutional and beyond its powers. Had the matter rested here, our government would have been in a dil mma. But Messrs Morse and Bowlin then abandoned the demand involved in the treaty, and presented t eir ultimatum. This was the immediate payment of $400,000 for the damages sustained by our citizens in the Panama riot. The New Granadian government not only rejected this demand, and reiterated the denial of its responsibility, but in a Cabinet Council it was unanimously resolved that the government of the United States was identified with its citizens in originating and aggravating the riot of the 15th of April, and to demand from it the payment of $150,000 for damages incurred. No resource was left to our Commissioners, and Mr. Morse left as soon as possible. Mr Bowlin, our Minister at Bogota, determined to remain some little time longer there, as a new administration was to go into power on the 1st of April under Senor Ospina, and it was desirable to give the new government an opp u-tunity to recede from its false position. This is the present state of affairs. As soon as Mr. Buchanan saw the position they had assumed, he very properly ordered our naval forces to concentrate at the Isthmus ports, in order to protect the vast interests of our citizens there. How little probability there is of the new President, Ospina, receding from the position taken by the present administration in New Granada, is evident I'rom several facts. In the mixed Cabinet, that has unanimously deter-

mined to assume the present attitude of that government, there are two persons who may have great influence with the incoming administration. Senor Gonzalez, the Attorney General, holds over by his constitutional tenor of office, aud General Ortega, the present Minister of War, was one of the most active and efficient supporters of Senor Ospina in the late Presidenti 1 1 canvass in that republic. To this we may add that the Granadian House of Ilepresen tatives, in which the conservatives þÿ þÿOspina s party þÿ have the majority, passed unanimously, on the 17th of March, a resolution app oving the course of that government and its Commissioners in the recent discussion with those of the United States. In view of these facts, and of the great interests we have at stake in the security of the Isthmus Transit at Panama, there remains but one course for our government to pursue. Any interruption of the present communication between our Atlantic and our Pacific possessions at this critical moment, would be a cause of innumerable mercantile disasters both here and in California, which would produce a commercial revulsion. The Isthmus of Panama is now passing through that transition that always attends the introduction of great improvements, and is in a state of industrial change. The completion of the railroad has destroyed the means of livelihood of thousands of muleteers, boatmen and laborers þÿ many of whom possessing the luxurious and dissolute habits engendered by the gold that flowed in upon them

during the first rush of emigration to California, are now destitute, without employment, and ready for any desperate adventure. Their eye is directed particularly against the railroad, which they look upon as the fruitful cause of all their evils ; and when we remember the scenes that took place not long since in the Erie excitement in Pennsylvania, it will be seen that their feeling is the result of general laws rather than of any peculiar ignorance on their part. Under all these circumstances there is but one course for our government to pursue. It must not only take immediate possession of the Isthmus of Panama, and guarantee the uninterrupted security of the transit to our citizens and to the world, but it must at once organize a stable and wise rule there, which shall place that security upon a permanent basis now and in the future events of the return of the district to New Granada. Leaving the course of action to one or two naval officers and the employes of the Panama Railroad, will not effect this purpose. Let it take no halfway measures and trust to luck, as poor Pierce did, or it will meet with poor þÿPierce fate. s Let it send out at once competent men to organize and administer a government there, and then, whether we keep the Isthmus or not, it will confer a great boon upon the civilized world

GOLD IN VENEZUELA. Considerable excitement has been caused here by the arrival of a vessel from the Spanish Alain, bringing letters and also a copy of the Guayana Gazette , containing extraordinary reports of the discovery of a new Gold field about 90 miles from Upata, where it will be recollected about 3 or 4 years ago a large quantity of gold was taken from the river. W have been favored with a sight of several of these letters, and also with a copy of a letter published in the Guayant Gazette ; one of these letters states that nearly all the clerks and laborers are leaving Ciudad Bolivar ! (Angostura) for the new Alines which are

i Nr. 44. at a place called Tupugen, and we understand formerly belonging to the late Colonel Hamilton þÿ that they are leaving in parties of 30 and 40 a day þÿ Dr. Plassart, with a detachment of soldiers has been nent by the Government to the Gold field to keep order. The river Steamers had been obliged to cease working, in consequence of all their hands having left and started lor the gold fields. The average find is two ounces per day for each man ; but there have been instances where much larger quantities have been taken. A Air. Gruber who left here some 2 years ago, obtained twenty-four ounces in between 7 and 8 hours; and 2 men who were working at the same time obtained forty-four ounces. This gold field is said to be within the British territory of British Guiana according to the line ran some years since by Sir Robert Schomburgh, by order of the British Government. Letters in town state that Air. Alatheson, her Britannic Majesty's Vice-Consul at Ciudad Bolivar has left that place and proceeded to the gold field ; the gold lies at a depth oi between 5 and 6 teet front the surface. Large orders have been received here for pickaxes, shovels, and other implements for digging. We see by the Domeratu Col.mist of the 22nd April, that a French Schooner had arrived from Cayenne, for the purpose of obtaining 1U0 laborers to take to that Colony where gold also has been found in considerable quantities. At that date the Detnerara papers had not heard of the discovery of gold on this side of their territory,

as the people can travel there by land, we fear it will have a bad effect upon their labouring population. PRUSSIA. According to letters from Berlin the bad faith of Prussia has again manifested itself by making new difficulties concerning the Neufchatel Treaty. It is stated that the King insisted on the original clause relative to the revision of the Constitution, and the article which refers to the Church. It results that the Neufchatel question after all lias not advanced so much as was expected towards a satisfactory solution. The Session of the Prussian Chambers was closed on the 12th inst., by a royal message read by M. de Manteuffel. The Message enumerates the various measures adopted during the session ; it mentions likewise the measures which have not passed ; it alludes to the bill relative to the prohibition of payments in foreign notes, and expresses the hope that a general understanding on that measure will be come to with other States. The Message expresses satisfaction at the conclusion of the negotiations for the settlement of the Sound Dues. The royal Message does not make any allusion to foreign politics. It is rumoured that the King of Prussia intends to go to Rome in the autumn, "as he is desirous of having some private and confidential conversation with his Holiness the Pope." His Majesty is said to have scruples of conscience on matters of religion, and his enemies insinuate that he fancies no one can so effectually remove them as the head of t he Roman Catholic Church. A learned German, when speaking in English of his Prussian Ministry, observed that a man of such a romantic
character, and with such " medieval" tendencies, was even capable of abdicating and embracing the Roman Catholic faith.

Bogota, March 9, 1857. PANAMA. British Consulate, | Panama, April 13, 1857. ) Sir, þÿ I thank you for the file of official ga zettes you were pleased to send me. In the number dated March 13, the correspondence between Messrs. Potnbo and Gonzales and M essrs. Morse and Bowlin, is published, in which I remark that allusions are made to the report which, at the instance of Mr I'ombo, I furnished in regard to the lamentable collision and deaths which took place on the 15th of April last year. Mr. Pombo having limited himself to quoting several passages of iny said report, it has been believed that I attempted to excuse or justify the bloody attack made that unfortunate night on the passengers who were in the railroad depot, and this obliges me to reproduce, literally, the paragraph from which these passages were extracted.

In answering Mr. T'ombo's interrogatory in regard to responsibility, I said : þÿ "As regards responsibility, my opinion is that the want of a sufficient military or police force in Panama, ill view of the peculiar situation of the Isthmus, makes this government responsible for any losses suffered by foreigners, who naturally expect from the government of the country where they reside, due protection for their lives and property. At the same time due allowance should be made for the state of excitement of the populace, and the repeated acis of brutaliiy they had suffered from the same class of California passengers." The above shows that my opinion was, that in granting a compensation due allowance should be made for the state of excitement of the natives ; but it never ente ed into my mind that any leniency should be shown the wretches who committed so many excesses on that occasion. To remove, therefor", all offensive imputations as to the uprightness of my character, I take the liberty to request that you will be pleased to order this note to be published in the next number of the Gaceta del E tado. Yours &c., WM. PERRY. To Sr. Bartoi.one Calvo, Governor of Panama.

CAPITULATION OF WALKER Most of the news from Walker comes through desertion from his army ; but our reporter yesterday saw a gentleman who never was in his service, and whose statements nre vouched for as entirely reliable. Tuis gentleman was Mr. John Vredeu burgh, late engineer of the steamer Ogden, one of tho vessels belonging to the Transit Company, which was seized by Spencer. He left the Island of Tortuga, Lake Nicaragua, on the 23 d of March, on his way to Puenta Arenas, on the Pacific. Before starting, ho heard that Walker was on the point of making a desperate attempt to leave the country. At Santa Rosa he saw two d-serters who had just escaped from Walker's eamp. They said that AValker had not more than 200 effective men in Iliva=, and that they were all absolutely starving, being hemmed in on nil sides by the enemy. The opposing force was between 3,0 JO and 4,00J men, well armed, and pro v id d with every requisite. On his way to Puenta Arenas, Mr. Vredenbnrgh says that he passed large numbers of deserters from the filli- I ustcr army, all of wfiom concurred in represer ting that Walker was in so desperate a straight that, could he get away, he would flee the country immediately. At Puenta Arenas which ho reached on the 10th of April, he learned that a rounder had arrived with the intelligence that Walker h id strongly fortified himself in a yard between two buildings, and that the allies were to make a decisive movement in a few days, if the fillibusters did not surrender. of the steamer Panama, on which Mr. Vredenburgh went to Panama, informed him that between La Union and Realejo he passed a brig and a schooner with 1,0 JO men on board, from Guatemala lor Nicaragua, and heard that another 1000 men from the same State were on their way to that country by land to join the Patriot army. The same gentleman states, from his own knowledge, that ever since Walker left Granada, so far from having fought the great battles, nnd gained the glorious victories which have been reported, he has lost every battle. CHINESE IMMIGRATION. To the Editor of the 'Times.' Sir, The letter from Mr. Thomas þÿ H. Gladstone which you published yesterday deserves the serious attention ol Her Majesty's Government, for the horrible degration to Cuba, and its consequences, scription lie therein gives of Chinese emi- is truly disgraceful to this country. British ships have until last year been engaged in transporting crowds of Chinese, without any regulation as to number, or space, or provisions, for the voyage from China to Havannah. And, though they are now subject to some control in these respects under the Act 14th and 19th of Victoria, cap. 104, it is obvious that Chinese Coolies when landed in Cuba, as apprentice-labourers, have no chance of being treated as freemen. The only regulation that can prove effectual for their protection is one which ought to be applied to all emigration, that no British ship shall be permitted to convey emigration to any country in which slavery prevails will degenerate into bondage as has been well exemplified by r. Gladstone from what he saw during his sojourn in Cuba. As Chinese have also been conveyed to the British West Indies, Air. Gladstone naturally invites inquiry respecting the manner in which they had been introduced, and the condition in which they are found in our own colonies ; and considering that the only effectual means of suppressing slavery is to render free labour practically cheaper within the tropics, as it is in Europe, I hope you will allow me to explain what has been done to make the experi-

ment of transferring free labourers from China to these fertile possessions. In the year 1851 the colonics of Guiana and Trinidad united to send an intelligent agent, under the sanction of the Home Government to China, for the purpose of ascertaining whether suitable labourers could be induced to emigrate to these colonies, and what arrangements would be necessary to conduct the emigration in a satisfactory manner. The agent employed, having been appointed by the Secretary of State, corresponded with the Emigration Commissioners, and a few extracts from their annual reports will show that the utmost care was taken to avoid mismanagement and to prevent abuse. " In all parts of China visited by Mr. White, the joint agent of British Guiana and Trinidad, the country is peopled to for the mere necessaries of life." excess, and there is a consequent struggle . . " Those Chinese with whom Mr White communicated expressed no disinclination to emigrate, and asked no questions, except

as to the rate of wages and the cost of living; they insisted, however, on an advance of money at starting, principally for the purpose of leaving it with their aged relatives, and stipulated for the power of making further remittances. In no case did they appear to contemplate receiving return passages to their country. " We stated in our last report that preliminary steps had been taken for setting on foot an emigration from China. Considerable delay occurred, arising, in the first instance, from the non-arrival in England of Mr. White, whose advice and services the West India Committee were justly anxious to secure before plunging into a new and delicate undertaking. " The whole number of Chinese hitherto introduced into the British West Indies is as follows; þÿ British Guiana, 647; Trinidad 958 ; Jamaica, 472,205 of which number came from Panama." Contrary to Mr. Gladstone's impression, it will be seen that the number of Chinese is inconsiderable. They have generally proved excellent labourers, and there is a great desire to continue the immigration, but there is even a stronger desire to commence the colonization of Chinese by bringing families, or at least young married couples. It is, indeed, alleged that the emigration of females is contrary to the lex scri/da of China. The same observation may he made in regard to the emigration of males, though thousands embark openly at all the principal ports throughout the year. Those who have promoted emigra-

tion from China have preferred adult males, because their purpose has been to obtain effective labourers. This is doubtless, also, the most urgent motive with our own planters, but their interests would lead them further to connect this object, even at some present expense, with the important benefit which would arise from the permanent settlement of an industrious and increasing population on their plantations. The British West India proprietors are in fact, the only parties who appear to be willing to encourage the emigration of Chinese women as well as men. It has however, been always difficult in the first period of any emigration to induce females to remove. And there is even now a great disparity of the sexes in our golden Australian colonies. In the emigration from Calcutta to the British West Indies the proportion of females has been annually increasing; and as having some bearing on the Chinese question I may here give the particulars of the emigration from that port to British Guiana during the last few months: þÿ Mules. Females. Children. Infanta VVellesley . . 254 84 24 20 Bucephalus . . . 252 84 29 15 Sir R. Sepping . 197 59 26 9 Roman Emperor 207 68 26 12 Total 910 295 105 66 These figures indicate a nearer approach to colonization than any previous experience. From China emigration to our colonies must be conducted under the Passengers' Act, 1819 Victoria, cap. 104. When the emigrants arrive in the West Indies they are, of course, under the guardianship of

the Governors appointed by the Crown, and are in the full enjoyment of all the privileges of British free labourers, presenting a perfect contrast to the miserable fate of their countrymen who are carried to Cuba. This discrepancy between statements and figures tends to prove that however zealous and active, Her Majesty's Commissioners possess no reliable data on this subject ; and that, whilst their reports are based upon such facts only as come to their knowledge through channels more or less equivocal,, they themselves have a conviction that the trade is carried on to a far greater extent than they are in a position to establish on evidence that would be deemed conclusive for official purposes. But on this point the Committee beg to submit further evidence. In the correspondence between the Spanish and the British Government on the subject of the abolition of the slave trade, it is stated that the local census returns exhibited a positive annual increase in the slave population, up to the year, 1843, of 110 fewer than 15,000. But the right honorable the Earl of Aberdeen, writing to Mr. Bulwer on the 31st of December 1843, states authoritatively that the census of 1841, which served as a basis for the foregoing estimate, was well known to be incorrect, and only a few thousands above the half of the actual slave population at the period it was taken ; for the most intelligent inhabitants of the island asserted that at that very time it amounted to between 800,000 and 900,000, although in 1821, the date of the previous census, it was set down at only 265,000. As the augmentation of the slaves by natural increase is merely nominal, whilst the mortality

is notoriously excessive, the fact above referred to furnishes conclusive evidence, that within a eriod of twenty years the slave population ad been nearly quadrupled, by illegal importations, at the annual average rate of upwards of 30,000. The Committee believe they may assert, upon evidence in every respect unexceptionable, that from 1841 to the close of 1853, at least 15,000 negroes have been annually added to the slave population. They would observe that 20,000 is estimated to be a low annual average, Assuming, however, the number officially reported to be correct, the Committee submit that these continued importations constitute a flagrant breach of international faith, and that the interests of humanity require that Her Majestys's Government should adopt decisive measures to ensure the fulfilment of the treaties into which Spain has entered with this country. The Committee would add, that this breach of faith is the more flagrant on the part of Spain, by reason of her having been paid out of the British Treasury, as an indemnity for the abandonment of the traffic, the large sum of <£400,000 ; which, with the interest thereupon, would now amount to upwards of a million and a quarter sterling. The Committee observe that her Majesty's Commissary Judge at the Havana has expressed the following : " That the law as it is, and as it is administered, is wholly inadequate to the correction of the crime of slave trading, and that this abominable traffic is not likely to be suppressed

until it has been declared piracy, and the penalty attaching thereto made to extend to the owners, outfitters, masters and crews of the vessels, and the whole class of agents engaged in it, to the owners of the negroes and their agents and brokers, as well as to the Lieutenant-Governor and officers of the districts where slaves may be landed, the fact of a disembarkation of slaves at any place being taken as presumptive evidence of the complicity of the parties referred to." The Committee have also noticed the efforts which, tinder instructions from your Lordship, Her Majesty's representative at Madrid has made to induce the Spanish Government to propose to the Cortes the enactment of a stringent law, making the slave trade piracy. That the Spanish Government rhould, up to the latest date on which the Committee possess information, not only not have taken a decisive step in this direction, but have sought to evade the question, excites no surprise in the mind of the Committee, seeing how scandalously that

S T , C R 0 I X X, V (j S Government has hitherto disregarded its most solemn engagements. Nevertheless, it may be considered as something gained, that the Spanish Minister for Foreign Affairs has announced that " the Spanish Cabinet does not reject the request set forth by her Britannic Majesty's Government, but only defers i s decision until it has collected the necessary data in order to ascertain win tlier it will be possible for it to make the declaration in question without putting in jeopardy the sacred interests which are entrust d to its loyalty." That no such danger as the Spanish Government affects to apprehend would r, suit from the measure suggested appears to be conclusively demonstrated by Mr. Consul Crawford, in his despatch to your Lordship, dated Havana, 3rd January, 1855, from which the Committee beg leave to quote an extract. He says : " The Spanish Government, if they really intend that the treaties with Great Britain shall be faithfully observed, and are desirous the slave trade need be under no apprehension in adopting the most stringent measures for that purpose : they have force enough at their command to suppress any semblance of dissatisfaction were tliev to declare slave trading to be piracy, and deal with it as such in all its branches and ramifications ; the measure, your Loidship may rest assured, will neither endanger their colony, nor alter its tranquility. I consider the allegation of such motives for not acceding to the request of her Majesty's Government as a mere pretext to put off the ex-

tinction of a barbarous and everywhere else detested traffic, which they know will always continue to be carried 011 ; and therefore I most respectfully submit to your Lordship's pressed to put an end to it the better " better judgment, that the sooner they are As her Majesty's Government appears to have arrived at the conclusion, that to declare and to constitute s'ave trading to be piracy is the only measure calculated to ensure its speedy suppression ; as this view also appears to be confirmed by her .Majesty's representatives at the Havana; and a- by this time the Cabinet ot Madrid must have received from Cuba full information on this subject, and be aware that the contemplated measure would not entail the disastrous results that were alleged ; the Committee would respectfully submit whether the time has not arrived when her Majesty's Government may press the Cabinet of Madrid for an immediate decision Another subject to which the Committee desire to call your Lordship's attention is the projected scheme for the importation into Cuba of from 40,000 to 50,000 Africans as apprentices, reference to which is made in the Annual Report for 1855 of Her Majesty's Commissary Judge at. the Havana, as having been then quite recently again under discussion. The C miuitke have received informatiuu that this scheme 1ms obtained the sanction of General Concha, who is stated to have even proposed to suppress the slave-trade in Cuba, provided the Cabinet of Madrid will graut biui the

exclusive privilege of hiring out, or assigning these aprcndices Aud the Committee are further informed that an agent, whose name the Committee are prepared to produce, lias been despatched to Europo to procure the assent of the French and the British Governments to this scheme, which agent was recently in Paris. Tl. eir sanction is sought with a view to enable the traders to repair to and to quit the African Coast without molestation But it is obvious that tli s nefarious project is iuteuded merely as a cover for prosecuting with impunity the traffic in our fcllowmen. Indeed, the parties to it do not scruple to avow their intention to carry it out with or without the sanction of the Governments referred to. Should the attempt prove successful, there can be 110 doubt that thes > socalled apremlices would be at once reduced to hopeless Slavery. It may be stated, that on the assignment ol the Africans thus introduced, the local authorities in Cuba are to receive a certain sum per head, by way of fee, as is done in the case of the etnaneipados, with a view to compensate them lor the loss of hush-money by the suppression of the trade in slaves. It is evident, that should this astute immigration scheme be carried out in defiance of the Government whose

sanction is sought, the parties will simply incur the risks of ordinary slave trading. If the vessels should be captured in the Cuban waters, as slavers they will be adjudicated by the Mixed- Commission Court in due course, aud the negroes assigned as cmancipados in the usual way Such aa may be taken through the efforts of the Captain-General, after they have been landed, will be subjected to the same ordeal, but lie will gain credit for activity in the suppression of the slavetrade, and the British Government will continue to be altogether deceived as to the extent to which it is prosecuted. It is to be presumed that many vessels would evade detection, as tlicy now do, and would, through the connivance of the local authorities, succeed in d.sembarking their human freight. Tho purchasers of the cargoes would then procure "cedulas" for the m as unregistered slaves, ou the payment of a comparatively suiall fee, or would altogether evade General Concha's new regulation, by submitting to a fine, as is notoriously done at tuis time to any exteut. It cannot but be obvious to your Lordship that such a scheme is open to the very severest condemnation, as fraught with the gravest objections. Apart from the fact that there is not, nor can there bo, a free emigration of negroes from Africa in the present condition of native society, it is well kuown that immigrants in Cuba are worse off than slaves, or than even the emancipating ; and that laws to regulate immigration to a slave-colony, however benevolently framed,

will inevitably be evaded. With reference to the measures that might be adopted for tho suppression of the slave trade, the Committee would observe, that until the system of Slavery is abolished in Cuba, tlieie must ever exist the strongest incentives to continue the traffic, and though it might be sensibly diminished were it made piracy, no measure short of emancipation is likely to bring it to an end. The Committee have ever advocated these views, and have, on various occasions, earnestly besought Her Majesty's Gqverntnent to require ot the Cabinet of Madrid that Spain should fulfil her treaty obligations with this country, and restore to liberty the uegroes who have been introduced into Cuba in violation of the most solemn engagements. It is demonstrable that the bulk of tho actual slave population in Cuba ha« been surreptitiously imported, and there is no question that it is entitled, under the treaties ot 1817 and 1835, to immediate and unconditional freedom. Were those treaties carina into effect therefore. Slavery would be virtually abolished, and the slave trade must come to an end. The Committee respectfully but earnestly submit to your L01 dsbip the propriety of bringing these views under the notice of the Spanish Government, and of urging their adoption, not only for the sake of a too long and deeply injured humanity, but for that of simple justice. The Committee beg, in conclusion, to acknowledge their appreciation of your Lordship's efforts for the suppression of the slave trade ge-

nerally, and to express their earnest hope, that, for the honour and credit of a nation professing the Christian religion, you will exert the influence attaching to your elevated position to bring this wicked system to an end, seeing that the responsibility of its continuance, in this instance, rests, in a great measure, with the Briti-h Government, in permitting that of Spain to persist in openly violating her solemn engagements. On behalf of the Committee. (Signed) Geo. W. Alexander, Chairman L A. Chamerovzow, Secretary

I NEVER FORGIVE. In the course of a voyage to America, Mr. Wesley heard General Oglethorpe, with whom he sailed, making a great noise in the cabin, upon which be stepped in to know the cause. The General immediately addressed him, saying, þÿ Mr. Wesley, you must excuse me. I have met with a provocation too great for a man to bear. You know the only wine I drink is Cyprus wine, as it agrees with me best of any ; I therefore provided myself with several dozens of it ; and this þÿvillain (his servant, who was present, almost dead with fear) þÿ has drank up the whole of it. But I will be revenged on him. I have ordered him to be tied hand and foot, and to be carried to the man-of-war which sails with us. The rascal should have taken care how he used me so, for I never þÿforgive. þÿ Then, þÿSir, said Mr. Wesley, looking calmly at him, þÿ I hope you never þÿsin. The General confounded at the reproof, threw his keys to the servant, and bade him do better in future. Here, then, is the point: if we would never forgive, we must never sin. The very proneness to sin which we find in ourselves should be a most powerful incentive to tbe cultivation of a spirit of forgiveness.

From the Illustrated Loudon News There can be no doubt as to the result of the new measure for the admission of Jews to Parliament, which has been introduced to the House of Commons by Lord Palmerston. It is understood that, this time, the question is a Ministerial one, which it ought to have been made before; and that, it defeated upon it, the Ministry will retire from office. The members of the House of Lords who have alone impeded the passing of similar measures in previous Sessions will hesitate this time to imperil the peace of the country by persistence in the obstructive policy which they have hitherto pursued, not so n.uch from their own strength as from the cowardice and weakness of the friends of the Jews. The House of Commons l as four times opened its door tor the admission of Baron Rothschild, four times elected as the representative of the city of London, and lour times the House of Lords has shut it in his face. If again excluded, the Baron lias pledged himself to the electors to resign his seat, and the electors have pledged themselves to the Baron to return him a filth time. These pledges will he redeemed. How long can such an unseemly contest be allowed to com inue ? The consciences of those rnemh us of the Upper House who have so successfully rest tod the wishes of the Hon -e of Common and the people on this point may he at rest as to their own share in the transaction. They have done enough for conscience' sake, and need not any longer contend against an overpowering necessity. The House of Lords claims

to be the sole judge of its own privihges. It indignantly resisted the introduction of Lord Wenshydaleto its bot ches, because it deemed its tights, its privileges, and the vital principles of its constitution, to be attacked or imperilled by the proposed creation of life peerages. The House of Commons will, if expedient, imitate the example, and declare itself the sole judge of its own rules, privileges, and constitution. In this case the inconvenient, if not scandalous, spectacle would he presented to the world of two of the great estates of the realm in a free country contending for the mastery. In such a contest the House of Lords must know that it would he hopeless to expect victory ; and should fear that defeat would not he unaccompanied by the penalties of loss in of character, stance, which all wars and conflicts or loss of subwhatever the defeated are certain, sooner or later, to be compelled to pay. But Lord I'almerston's measure, aided by his determination to carry it, will, there is every reason to hope, incline the Lords to confirm the decision of the Commons, and thus end peacefully and satisfactorily a conflict which has already lasted too long. It is true wisdom to know when to yield ; and of this wisdom the House of Lords, on several much more trying and important occasions, has shown that it is not deficient. That House stands deservedly high in public estimation, and it will not forfeit its character for prudence and patriotism by carrying on a contest which the House of
Commons, backed by the city of London and the majority of the people, will once more prove to he useless.

We hope soon to receive an extract of these accounts for publication, in accordance with the $6 of the Colonial Law and the 22 of the Communal Law ; we however beg leave to remark, that a more intellegible extract, than that usually published, is one which the public has a right to expect ; for no one can have t.he least idea of the amount of sing'e or individual expenses when so condensed under general heads.
